plot_extraction.response_text:
Bill Burtenshaw, a deeply superstitious former sailor, drinks heavily and squanders his wages and household possessions, leaving his wife impoverished. When his old shipmate Silas Winch visits, Mrs. Burtenshaw tells him about Bill’s alcoholism and recalls the two men’s pact that whichever died first would return as a ghost. She and Silas devise a plan for Silas to impersonate his own drowned ghost and frighten Bill into sobriety.

Silas appears beside the drunken Bill’s bed covered in luminous paint. Convinced that his supposedly dead friend has returned, Bill swears never to drink again. Exploiting the deception, Silas also makes him promise to send fifteen shillings each week to Silas’s alleged widow. Bill quits drinking and faithfully sends the money, but his wife becomes furious that so much of their income is going to Silas and cannot expose the trick without risking Bill’s relapse or anger.

She eventually stages a second ghostly visitation, pretending that Silas’s ghost has appeared to her because a payment was lost. She claims the ghost ordered her to deliver the weekly money personally. Bill thereafter gives the fifteen shillings directly to his wife, believing she is taking it to the widow. He remains sober, while she keeps the money and uses it to buy the clothes and hats she had previously been unable to afford.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the manner of a comic oral yarn, framed by a night-watchman who addresses an implied listener and uses a personal anecdote to illustrate a supposedly general truth. His opening reflections on superstition lead casually into the embedded tale, and the frame gives the narrative the air of an improvised dockside performance rather than a polished literary account. The speaker’s questionable logic, suppressed irritation with the cat, and confident moralising immediately establish him as a humorous and not entirely reliable raconteur.

The dominant linguistic feature is heavily marked working-class vernacular. Pronunciation is represented through eye dialect and dropped consonants—“’ad,” “’im,” “arter,” “ses,” “wot,” “agin,” and “fust”—along with colloquial contractions, nonstandard grammar, nautical expressions, and idioms such as “three sheets in the wind.” This phonetic spelling creates a strong speaking voice, locates the tale socially, and sustains the impression that it is being told aloud. The narration and dialogue share much of the same idiom because the entire embedded story is filtered through the watchman’s voice. Repetition, self-correction, loose coordination, and phrases such as “as I said afore” further imitate spontaneous speech.

Dialogue drives most of the action. Exchanges are brisk, plainly phrased, and built around repetition with small comic variations. Bill’s terrified “Good-by,” Silas’s increasingly elaborate ghostly instructions, and Mrs. Burtenshaw’s practical stage-management of the groans all gain force from timing rather than descriptive complexity. Speech tags are deliberately repetitive—especially “ses”—which reinforces the storyteller’s oral rhythm and keeps attention on the verbal contest between characters. Interrupted phrases, stammering, emphatic questions, and dashes reproduce fear, hesitation, and comic escalation.

The humour is dry, ironic, and frequently deadpan. Absurd or cruel details are delivered as though they were perfectly reasonable: a ghost dislodges a drowned cabin-boy from his leg, Silas is asked to vary his groans like a performer, and Bill’s alcoholism is described as the natural consequence of earning enough to support only a wife. Much of the comedy comes from incongruity between solemn supernatural language and mundane material interests. The apparent haunting begins as a scheme to reform Bill, is hijacked by Silas to obtain fifteen shillings a week, and is then reclaimed by Mrs. Burtenshaw through a second fraudulent visitation. The narrator seldom explains the joke; understatement and literal-minded phrasing allow the irony to emerge on its own.

Characterisation is economical and behavioural. Bill is drunken, credulous, selfish, and cowardly, but his fear makes him obedient. Silas is introduced as gloomy and superstitious, then revealed as opportunistic beneath his pose of charitable concern. Mrs. Burtenshaw initially appears long-suffering and vulnerable, yet proves the most adaptable and strategically intelligent character. Their motives are shown through actions, bargaining, and speech rather than psychological analysis. Recurring physical details—the bedclothes, hidden head, luminous paint, groans, poker, and weekly money order—function as comic props and make the domestic setting theatrical.

The plot is tightly constructed around reversal and escalating deception. A preliminary chain of anecdotes establishes superstition as the comic premise. The central scheme then unfolds in clear stages: Silas proposes the false haunting, Bill is difficult to wake, the performance finally succeeds, the moral warning becomes financial extortion, and Mrs. Burtenshaw discovers that her intended cure has cost her money. The final counter-trick mirrors the first haunting but reverses control. She imitates a conversation with the invisible ghost, exploits Bill’s inability to look, and redirects the weekly payment to herself. This symmetrical structure gives the ending the neatness of a practical joke or folktale.

Pacing alternates between compressed summary and extended scene. Years of drinking and marital difficulty are covered quickly, while the bedroom haunting is rendered almost moment by moment. The prolonged failure to wake Bill delays the expected confrontation and turns suspense into farce. Later, his repeated retreats beneath the bedclothes provide a visual rhythm, while Silas’s increasingly specific demands steadily reveal the true object of the deception. The second haunting is shorter because it repeats an already established pattern, allowing the conclusion to arrive sharply.

The prose uses simple syntax, concrete detail, and cumulative clauses suited to spoken narration. Descriptions are brief but vivid, particularly Silas’s luminous face, wet hair, and resonant groans. Figurative language is mostly colloquial and exaggerated—noise that “froze the marrer” in the bones, a room-shaking groan, and a warning “fifty million times worse than pink rats.” Hyperbole is treated as ordinary speech, intensifying both the narrator’s personality and the farcical atmosphere.

The thematic treatment of superstition is deliberately paradoxical. Superstition is irrational, yet it produces practical results: Bill stops drinking, becomes healthier, and supports his household, albeit under false pretences. Deception is similarly ambiguous. Every major character manipulates someone else, but the final arrangement is presented less as a moral scandal than as rough domestic justice. The closing sentence delivers the punch line by translating the supernatural plot into the everyday reward of hats and clothes. Overall, the style combines vernacular realism, oral storytelling, domestic farce, restrained satire, and a precisely engineered comic twist.

Superstitious people, said the night-watchman, lowering his voice and looking hard at the black cat by the warehouse door, is mostly people wot ought to know better. Sailormen is the worst, but I’ve known landsmen as could give ’em points and beat ’em easy. I knew a carpenter once as wouldn’t drive the last nail into a coffin on a Friday, not if you was to offer ’im overtime; but he’d walk under ladders all day without turning a hair. That shows you wot superstition is. It ain’t reason, and it ain’t sense. It’s knowing where to draw the line.

The cat got up, stretched itself, and came towards him.

“Git away,” said the watchman, without looking at it. “I don’t mind cats, black or any other colour. Only this one’s got no business ’ere.”

He shifted his stool a little farther from the warehouse door and folded his arms.

“I’ve ’eard,” he continued, “that if a black cat crosses your path it means either good luck or bad luck, according to whether it’s going to the right or the left. Nobody seems to know which, and by the time you’ve found out the cat’s gone ’ome. Sailormen don’t leave things undecided like that. They know exactly wot’s unlucky. Whistling at sea is unlucky; sailing on Friday is unlucky; cutting your nails in a calm is unlucky; and seeing a red-’aired woman afore breakfast is enough to make some of ’em turn back and spend the day in bed. That’s why red-’aired women mostly get their shopping done in the afternoon.

“I was at sea myself for over twenty year, and I never believed in none of it. Never. I’ve seen things, mind you, as couldn’t be explained by ordinary means, but that’s different. There was a hand come up out of a bucket aboard the *Mary Ann* one night, and beckon to the cook. Three men saw it, besides the cook, and next morning the cook found his best shirt missing. You may call that superstition if you like; I call it dishonesty. One of the three men was wearing the shirt when we reached Gravesend.

“Then there was the mate of the *Sea Pigeon*, who always said he could hear bells ringing under the water whenever a ship was going to sink. He heard ’em regular for fourteen years, and the ship never sunk once. At last the skipper found out it was two empty medicine bottles knocking together under the mate’s bunk. The mate said that didn’t prove nothing, and p’raps it didn’t. It only proves that some men would sooner believe a ghost than move their luggage.

“Still, superstition can be useful at times. I knew a man once as was cured of drinking by a ghost, and the curious part of it was that the ghost wasn’t dead. Not at the time, anyway. Whether he’s dead now I can’t say; he owed me half a crown when I last saw ’im, and people like that generally live to a great age.

“His name was Bill Burtenshaw, and a better sailor never stepped, so long as he was sober. When he wasn’t sober he couldn’t step anywhere without assistance. He was a thick-set man with a red face, a little brown beard, and a pair of eyes that always looked as if they’d just heard something behind ’em. He’d been at sea since he was twelve, and he’d collected superstitions the way other men collects foreign stamps. He wouldn’t sleep with his boots pointing towards the door; he wouldn’t pass a churchyard without touching iron; and if he heard a dog howl at night he’d stay awake till morning, unless he happened to be drunk, in which case you might have fired the dog out of a cannon beside ’is ear without disturbing him.

“Bill married a quiet little woman named Martha. She was the sort o’ woman as says very little because she’s busy thinking of things the man ought to ’ave thought of first. When Bill was courting, he brought ’er silk handkerchiefs, parrots’ feathers, shells, foreign scent, and once a little stuffed crocodile, which he said was useful as well as ornamental, though he never said wot for. Arter they was married he brought ’er nothing but excuses, and most of them second-hand.

“He earned good money. That was the trouble. If he’d earned twelve shillings a week, he might ’ave been a steady, respectable man; but he earned enough to keep a wife, and so he took to drink. He started on Saturday night, rested a little on Sunday morning, and went on again Sunday afternoon to make up for it. Monday he was sorry, Tuesday he was thirsty, Wednesday he was cheerful, and by Thursday Mrs. Burtenshaw was wondering which article of furniture would go next.

“He begun with things he called unnecessary. The parlour clock went because, he said, there was a clock at the church. The easy-chair went because sitting down too much was bad for a woman’s figure. Then the china dog off the mantelpiece went because it was unlucky to keep an animal as couldn’t bark. Arter that the spare blankets went, a copper kettle, three saucepans, and a pair of curtains. When Mrs. Burtenshaw asked ’im where the curtains was, he said they’d been sent to be cleaned, and when she asked which cleaners he got offended and went out.

“At last there was hardly enough left in the house to furnish a cupboard. Mrs. Burtenshaw kept the poker in the bedroom at night, partly for protection and partly because Bill hadn’t thought of selling it. She hid the flat-irons under a loose board, kept the teaspoons in her pocket, and wore two petticoats because she didn’t trust the chest of drawers.

“One evening, while Bill was out improving the landlord’s business, there came a knock at the door. Mrs. Burtenshaw opened it and saw a long, melancholy-looking man with sandy whiskers and a mouth that turned down at both corners as if life had disappointed ’im personal.

“‘Mrs. Burtenshaw?’ he ses.

“‘Yes,’ she ses.

“‘My name’s Silas Winch,’ he ses. ‘Me and Bill was shipmates aboard the *Golden Fleece*.’

“‘Come in,’ she ses, ‘if you don’t want nothing.’

“Silas looked a bit hurt at that, but he came in and sat down on the only chair. Mrs. Burtenshaw sat on an empty flour-bin.

“‘Bill out?’ he ses.

“‘Yes,’ she ses.

“‘At the Sailor’s Return?’ he ses.

“‘No,’ she ses. ‘At the Jolly Mariner.’

“‘Ah,’ ses Silas, nodding. ‘He always did like a change.’

“He looked round the room, which didn’t take long, and asked whether they’d moved lately.

“‘No,’ ses Mrs. Burtenshaw. ‘The furniture has.’

“Then she told ’im about Bill. She told ’im about the wages and the public-house, the blankets and the saucepans, and the clock that was no longer required because of the church. Silas listened with his mouth turned down worse than ever, and every now and then he shook his head till his whiskers brushed his coat.

“‘Drink,’ he ses at last, ‘is a terrible thing.’

“‘It is when somebody else does it,’ ses Mrs. Burtenshaw.

“‘I never touch it,’ ses Silas, ‘except when I’m asked.’

“Mrs. Burtenshaw said she’d remember not to ask ’im.

“Silas sat thinking, with his long hands between his knees. Then all of a sudden he looked up.

“‘Is Bill still superstitious?’ he ses.

“‘Worse,’ she ses. ‘Last week he gave my washing money to an old woman because she told ’im his left eyebrow meant sudden danger.’

“‘Did it?’ ses Silas.

“‘It did when he came ’ome,’ ses Mrs. Burtenshaw.

“Silas rubbed his hands together very slow.

“‘Me and Bill made an agreement once,’ he ses. ‘It was aboard the *Golden Fleece*, off the coast of Peru, or p’raps it was Margate. Wherever it was, the weather was very bad. We agreed that whichever of us died first was to come back and tell the other wot it was like.’

“Mrs. Burtenshaw stared at ’im.

“‘Did you put it in writing?’ she ses.

“‘No,’ ses Silas. ‘Ghosts don’t care for paperwork. But Bill remembers. He was that frightened arterwards that he made me promise not to come back during meals.’

“He leaned nearer and lowered his voice.

“‘If Bill was to think I was dead,’ he ses, ‘and if my ghost was to appear to ’im and warn ’im against drink—’

“Mrs. Burtenshaw sat up.

“‘Could you look dead?’ she ses.

“Silas considered. ‘I’ve been told I do of a morning,’ he ses.

“They talked it over. At first Silas wanted to appear in chains, but Mrs. Burtenshaw said chains cost money and made too much noise. Then he thought of a white sheet, but she said Bill knew their sheets had all been pawned. At last Silas said he knew a scene-painter at a little theatre who had some luminous paint left over from a demon. He could put it on his face and hands, wet his hair, and wear an old sea-cloak.

“‘You’ll ’ave to groan,’ ses Mrs. Burtenshaw.

“‘I can groan,’ ses Silas, drawing a long breath and giving one.

“Mrs. Burtenshaw jumped.

“‘Not like that,’ she ses. ‘That sounds as if you’d eaten something. Make it more lonely.’

“He tried again.

“‘Too cheerful,’ she ses.

“He tried a third time, beginning low and ending with a sort of wobble.

“‘That’s better,’ she ses. ‘It gave me quite a turn near the end. Do that one when he pulls the bedclothes over his head.’

“They settled it for the following Saturday. Silas was to spread a report that he’d been washed overboard from a barge in the river. Mrs. Burtenshaw was to tell Bill, and when Bill came ’ome drunk she was to leave the kitchen window open and the back door unbolted. Silas was to come upstairs at midnight, wake Bill, reform ’im, and go.

“‘Nothing about money,’ ses Mrs. Burtenshaw.

“‘Certainly not,’ ses Silas, looking shocked. ‘This is friendship.’

“Saturday came, and the story about Silas being drowned reached Bill by seven o’clock. It reached ’im in the Jolly Mariner, where four men told it four different ways. One said Silas had fallen overboard; one said he’d jumped; one said a rope had knocked ’im in; and the fourth said it was a barrel of cement. Bill believed all of ’em.

“He drank two glasses to Silas’s memory and another because Silas wouldn’t have wanted ’im to grieve. Then he remembered the agreement and turned pale under the red.

“‘He can’t come yet,’ he ses. ‘He’s only just drowned.’

“‘Depends on the tide,’ ses one of the men.

“Bill looked over his shoulder, swallowed his drink, and ordered another to keep the cold out. By closing-time the cold was out, and so was nearly everything else. Two men took ’im home and leaned ’im against his own door. Mrs. Burtenshaw got ’im upstairs by pushing from behind, took off one boot, gave up the other, and put ’im to bed crossways.

“Just afore midnight there was a soft tap at the kitchen window.

“Mrs. Burtenshaw went down, and there was Silas in the yard. His face shone pale green, his hands shone too, and his wet hair hung over his forehead. He had seaweed on one shoulder and a piece of string round his neck.

“‘Wot’s the string for?’ she whispers.

“‘I was going to ’ave an anchor on it,’ he whispers back, ‘but it was too heavy.’

“‘Take your boots off,’ she ses. ‘Ghosts don’t squeak.’

“He took ’em off and followed her upstairs. At the bedroom door she reminded ’im of the groan.

“‘The lonely one?’ he whispers.

“‘Yes. And don’t overdo it.’

“She went into the little back room and left ’im.

“Silas entered the bedroom. There was a candle burning on the washstand, and Bill lay on his back, snoring hard enough to shake the water in the jug. Silas stood beside the bed, folded his arms, and groaned.

“Bill went on snoring.

“Silas groaned again, louder.

“Bill gave a snort, stopped for a moment, and then started again with renewed strength.

“Silas leaned over ’im.

“‘Bill!’ he ses, in a deep sepulchral voice.

“Bill opened his mouth wider, but nothing else happened.

“Silas poked ’im in the shoulder with one luminous finger. Bill brushed it away and muttered something about five minutes more.

“Silas poked again.

“‘Bill Burtenshaw!’ he ses. ‘Awake and behold!’

“Bill opened one eye, saw the shining face, and shut it again.

“‘Go away,’ he ses.

“Silas wasn’t prepared for that.

“‘Bill!’ he ses. ‘It is me—Silas Winch—returned from the bottom of the sea.’

“Bill pulled the bedclothes over his head.

“‘Good-by, Silas,’ he ses, muffled.

“‘Come out and look at me,’ ses Silas.

“‘I can see you very well where I am,’ ses Bill.

“Silas gave the lonely groan. Mrs. Burtenshaw, listening next door, thought it sounded a bit irritated, but Bill began trembling till the bedstead rattled.

“‘Wot do you want?’ he ses.

“‘I have come with a warning,’ ses Silas. ‘A terrible warning from them regions where the waves is always roaring and there ain’t no public-houses.’

“Bill gave a little cry.

“‘Don’t say that,’ he ses.

“‘I was washed overboard,’ continued Silas, warming to his work. ‘Down I went—down and down—past fishes with eyes like lamps, and a cabin-boy that had been there since eighteen-sixty-four. He caught hold of my leg, but I kicked ’im off.’

“‘Poor little chap,’ ses Bill from under the clothes.

“‘He was a nuisance,’ ses Silas. ‘Arter that I came to a dark gate, and a voice ses: “Silas Winch, return to earth and warn Bill Burtenshaw.”’

“‘Why me?’ ses Bill.

“‘Because of the drink,’ ses Silas. ‘Every glass you takes is another link in a chain wot you’ll ’ave to wear for ever and ever, and each link weighs fourteen pounds.’

“Bill’s teeth knocked together.

“‘I’ll stop,’ he ses. ‘I swear I’ll stop this very minute.’

“‘Not another drop?’ ses Silas.

“‘Not another drop.’

“‘Not even when it’s raining?’

“‘No.’

“‘Nor on your birthday?’

“‘No.’

“‘Nor when somebody else is paying?’

“There was a pause.

“‘No,’ ses Bill faintly.

“Silas groaned again, more comfortable now, and turned as if to go. Then he stopped. It had come into his mind that a man who was giving up drink would have a lot of spare money, and Silas always had ideas quick where spare money was concerned.

“‘There is one thing more,’ he ses.

“Bill made a miserable noise.

“‘I have left behind me,’ ses Silas, ‘a widow.’

“‘You wasn’t married,’ ses Bill, forgetting his fear for a moment.

“‘We kept it quiet,’ ses Silas. ‘Very quiet. Her name is—er—Jane.’

“‘Jane wot?’

“‘Jane Winch,’ ses Silas severely. ‘Naturally.’

“‘Where does she live?’ ses Bill.

“Silas hadn’t thought of that.

“‘A long way off,’ he ses. ‘So far that it would be no use your calling. She is poor, Bill. Very poor. Sitting at this moment in a room with no fire, no food, and three little children asking when father is coming ’ome.’

“‘Three?’ ses Bill. ‘You’ve been busy.’

“Silas groaned so fierce that Bill disappeared farther under the bedclothes.

“‘You must send her ten shillings a week,’ ses Silas.

“Then he thought again.

“‘Fifteen,’ he ses. ‘Ten for food and five for—other things.’

“‘That’s a lot,’ ses Bill.

“Silas bent down till his glowing face was close to the lump under the blankets.

“‘Down below,’ he ses, ‘there’s things fifty million times worse than anything a man sees after drinking. Things with horns, Bill. And tails. And eyes all over ’em.’

“‘I’ll send it,’ ses Bill quickly.

“‘Every week?’

“‘Every week.’

“‘By money order, payable to Mrs. Jane Winch?’

“‘Yes.’

“‘And write “From a friend” on the form.’

“‘Yes.’

“‘Good-by, Bill.’

“‘Good-by, Silas.’

“Silas gave one last groan, which Mrs. Burtenshaw afterwards said was the best of the evening, and crept downstairs. He had just got his boots on when she came after ’im.

“‘Wot was all that about fifteen shillings?’ she ses.

“‘A little extra touch,’ ses Silas. ‘Made it natural.’

“‘Natural?’ she ses. ‘You said nothing about a widow.’

“‘A ghost must ’ave responsibilities,’ ses Silas. ‘Besides, if Bill sacrifices something, the lesson’ll sink in deeper.’

“Mrs. Burtenshaw stared at ’im, but she couldn’t speak too loud for fear of Bill hearing. Silas promised to explain another time and went off through the yard, glowing gently in the dark.

“The cure worked. Bill woke next morning with one boot on and a dreadful memory. He searched the room for wet footprints, and when he found a smear of luminous paint on the bedpost he turned so white that Mrs. Burtenshaw nearly felt sorry for ’im.

“‘Silas came last night,’ he ses.

“‘Nonsense,’ she ses.

“‘I saw ’im.’

“‘You saw the drink,’ she ses.

“‘He was shining,’ ses Bill. ‘And wet. He’d been right down to the bottom. There was a cabin-boy hanging on to ’is leg.’

“Mrs. Burtenshaw said that ought to teach ’im not to drink on an empty stomach.

“But Bill was changed. He passed the Jolly Mariner that night without going in. The landlord came to the door and asked if he was ill, and Bill crossed the road. On payday he brought all his wages home, except fifteen shillings, and Mrs. Burtenshaw’s heart gave a jump till she remembered the widow.

“Next morning Bill bought a money order and sent it to the address Silas had given ’im. Silas had arranged for the letters to go to a small shop kept by a cousin of his, who didn’t ask questions because Silas owed ’im money too.

“Week arter week Bill sent the fifteen shillings. He never touched drink. His face lost some of its colour, his hands stopped shaking, and he began getting up in time for breakfast. He even brought home a small table to replace one he’d sold, though Mrs. Burtenshaw said it didn’t match anything, and Bill said there wasn’t anything left for it to match.

“You might think she’d have been pleased, and she was—at first. But fifteen shillings is fifteen shillings, whether it goes on drink or to a man painted green. Every Friday Bill counted it out with a solemn face.

“‘Poor Jane,’ he’d ses.

“‘Poor me,’ Mrs. Burtenshaw would ses.

“‘She’s got three children,’ ses Bill.

“‘So Silas told you,’ she ses.

“‘And no fire.’

“‘She ought to burn one of the children,’ ses Mrs. Burtenshaw. ‘It’d save food as well.’

“Bill was shocked. He said sorrow had made her hard.

“Mrs. Burtenshaw went to see Silas. She found ’im in a new waistcoat, smoking a large cigar.

“‘You’re looking well for a drowned man,’ she ses.

“‘A clear conscience,’ ses Silas.

“She demanded the fifteen shillings back. Silas said it was being spent on the widow. When she asked where the widow was, he tapped his chest and said she was there, meaning, he explained, that he carried her interests close to his heart.

“‘You cheated me,’ ses Mrs. Burtenshaw.

“‘I cured Bill,’ ses Silas. ‘Doctors charge money.’

“‘Not to the patient’s wife they don’t.’

“‘Somebody has to pay,’ ses Silas.

“She threatened to tell Bill the whole story, but Silas only smiled. He said Bill would either go back to drink from disappointment or throw them both into the river, and Mrs. Burtenshaw knew enough of Bill to see that there was sense in it. She went ’ome thinking.

“For six more weeks the money went. Bill grew stouter and Silas grew smarter. Mrs. Burtenshaw had two new dresses in her mind and not a penny to put on ’em. Then one Friday Bill came ’ome upset. The money order sent the week afore had been returned because of something wrong with the address.

“‘Jane never got it,’ he ses, staring at the envelope.

“Mrs. Burtenshaw stared too. Then she saw her chance.

“That night, just after they’d gone to bed, she sat up sudden.

“‘Who’s there?’ she ses.

“Bill sat up too.

“‘Wot is it?’ he ses.

“Mrs. Burtenshaw looked towards the foot of the bed and gave a little scream.

“‘Silas!’ she ses.

“Bill went under the bedclothes so quick he took most of them with ’im.

“‘Don’t look, Bill,’ ses Mrs. Burtenshaw. ‘He’s shining worse than ever.’

“From beneath the blankets came a sound like a mouse asking for mercy.

“Mrs. Burtenshaw listened to the empty room.

“‘Wot’s that, Silas?’ she ses. ‘The money was lost? Jane and the children is starving?’

“Bill groaned.

“‘No, Silas,’ she went on, ‘Bill didn’t do it on purpose. Don’t point at ’im like that. And put that chain down—you’ll damage the floor.’

“‘Ask ’im wot he wants,’ whispers Bill.

“‘Wot do you want, Silas?’ ses Mrs. Burtenshaw. Then she nodded slowly. ‘I see. You don’t trust the post no more. You want the fifteen shillings given to me every week, and I’m to take it to Jane personal.’

“‘That’s a long way,’ ses Bill, still hidden.

“Mrs. Burtenshaw held up her hand.

“‘Hush! He’s getting angry. Yes, Silas, I’ll take it. Every Saturday morning. And you’ll never trouble Bill again?’

“She paused.

“‘He ses he won’t,’ she told the blankets. ‘He’s going now.’

“Then she drew a long, lonely groan. It wasn’t quite so good as Silas’s, but Bill was in no condition to judge. She crept out of bed, opened the door, shut it softly, and came back.

“‘He’s gone,’ she ses.

“Bill put one eye out.

“‘Did he look bad?’ he ses.

“‘Terrible,’ she ses. ‘There was seaweed all over ’im, and the cabin-boy was back on his leg.’

“From that week onward Bill gave the fifteen shillings to his wife, and she went out every Saturday morning to deliver it. She always took a large shopping-bag, because appearances is important, and she stayed away long enough to reach the imaginary widow and come back.

“Bill never drank again. He remained sober, respectable, and frightened, which is as good a combination as you’ll find in a husband. Silas kept out of his way, and Mrs. Burtenshaw never told either of ’em more than was necessary.

“And that,” concluded the night-watchman, as the black cat rubbed itself against his boot and made him start, “shows you that superstition ain’t always a bad thing if it’s handled by somebody with sense. Bill got his health, Silas got several weeks at fifteen shillings, and Mrs. Burtenshaw got the rest.

“She spent most of it on clothes, and every time Bill saw her in a new hat he said it was wonderful how far a careful woman could make money go.”

# The Cartographer of Lost Roads

On the morning the road disappeared, Mara Vale was drawing it.

She sat at the kitchen table with a ruler in one hand and a mug of cold tea in the other, copying the old route from memory. It began behind the abandoned chapel, crossed the north meadow, and climbed through a stand of black pines before reaching the ridge. Beyond the ridge stood the blue house where her brother had once lived.

Mara drew the final curve, pressed her pencil down to mark the house, and heard a knock at the door.

The village postman stood outside, breathing hard.

“You’d better come,” he said.

Mara took her coat.

The road behind the chapel had vanished.

There was no broken stone, no wheel track, no grass-covered suggestion of where it had been. The north meadow stretched unmarked from the chapel wall to the pines. Even the hedges that had bordered the route now grew together in a seamless green line.

A crowd had gathered. Mr. Bell from the bakery insisted the road had run to the east. The schoolmistress claimed it had begun beside the graveyard gate. Old Mrs. Lorne said there had never been a road at all.

“There was,” Mara said.

Everyone turned toward her.

It was natural that they should. Mara was the village cartographer, though the village had little need of one. The coast lay to the west, the mountains to the east, and the streets of Vale’s Crossing had not changed in two hundred years. Still, she maintained the official maps, marked new wells and fallen bridges, and drew property lines when neighbors quarreled.

She also collected lost things.

Not gloves or coins. Lost paths. Forgotten alleys. Stairways bricked behind plaster. She mapped shortcuts remembered only by children and lanes abandoned after storms. In the attic of her cottage, hundreds of maps lay rolled in cedar boxes.

Now she looked across the meadow and felt an old fear move inside her.

“Did anyone travel the road yesterday?” she asked.

No one answered.

Mara turned to the postman. “You used to deliver letters to the blue house.”

He stared at her. “What blue house?”

“My brother’s house. Beyond the ridge.”

“You don’t have a brother.”

The villagers looked away with the embarrassed kindness people showed when grief made someone foolish.

Mara returned home alone.

In the attic, she opened the largest cedar box. It contained a single map, drawn on linen and stitched at the edges. At its center was Vale’s Crossing. Roads branched outward in black ink, some dark and solid, others pale as smoke. The vanished road was still there, but its line had faded overnight.

Mara touched it.

A memory came to her: a summer evening twelve years earlier, her brother Elias walking backward along the road, laughing as he carried a basket of apples.

You’ll fall, she had warned.

Then you’ll have to remember me kindly, he had replied.

She remembered the blue house. She remembered rain on its windows and copper pots in its kitchen. She remembered Elias marrying a woman named Nessa, whose hair was red and whose songs made dogs howl. She remembered their daughter, Lio, born during a thunderstorm.

Yet when Mara tried to picture Elias’s face, she saw only fog.

On the map, the road faded further.

“No,” she whispered.

She packed chalk, twine, a compass, bread, a lantern, and the linen map. Then she walked to the chapel.

The villagers had dispersed. Evening shadows filled the meadow.

Mara stood where the road should have begun. She closed her eyes and recalled every journey she had taken along it. Seventy-three paces north. A bend beside a stone shaped like a sleeping fox. A shallow ditch. A hawthorn tree split by lightning.

She opened her eyes and stepped forward.

At first there was only grass. Then, under her boot, she felt stone.

She marked the place with chalk and took another step. Stone again. She tied her twine to the chapel fence and continued into the meadow, following what memory told her was there.

After seventy-three paces, she turned north.

The sleeping fox stone appeared at dusk.

It did not rise from the earth gradually. One moment there was grass; the next, the gray stone stood beside her, silver with lichen. As Mara touched it, the meadow behind her blurred. The chapel’s roof faded into mist.

She lit her lantern.

Ahead, the lost road emerged beneath the grass, one pale stone at a time.

Mara walked until darkness swallowed the village.

The split hawthorn came next, though it was no longer dead. White blossoms covered its branches, glowing in the lantern light. Beneath it sat a boy in a red coat.

He was perhaps ten years old. His feet were bare.

“You took your time,” he said.

“Who are you?”

“Jonas.”

“Are you lost?”

“Not anymore.”

The answer made Mara uneasy. “Where are your parents?”

The boy pointed along the road. “Everywhere but here.”

Mara gave him bread. He ate quickly, watching her map.

“You shouldn’t carry that openly,” he said.

“Why?”

“The Collector dislikes competition.”

“I’m not competing with anyone.”

Jonas laughed. “Everyone who remembers is competing with him.”

A wind stirred the hawthorn blossoms. They lifted into the air, but instead of falling, they became white moths and flew east.

Mara looked back. Her twine vanished into darkness.

“Do you know the blue house?” she asked.

“There are many blue houses.”

“This one belonged to Elias Vale.”

The boy’s face changed.

“You should go home,” he said.

“So you know him.”

“I know the Collector took a man with that name.”

Mara knelt. “Took him where?”

Jonas pointed toward the pines.

“To the House of Unremembering.”

The black pines stood closer than they should have, crowding both sides of the road. Their branches interlocked overhead. Mara walked beneath them with Jonas at her heels.

He refused to explain who the Collector was. Whenever she asked, he whistled or kicked stones. At last she stopped.

“I need to know what I’m facing.”

Jonas studied her.

“People think forgetting is empty,” he said. “It isn’t. Forgotten things have to go somewhere. A song leaves your head. A face falls out of history. A path disappears because no one walks it. They all come here.”

“And the Collector?”

“He says he keeps them safe.”

“But?”

“But a cage can be safe.”

The forest whispered around them. Mara heard fragments in the wind: half a melody, an unfinished prayer, someone calling a name she almost recognized.

Jonas drew closer.

“He collects roads because roads lead back,” he said. “He collects names because names unlock doors. He collects people when they’re nearly forgotten.”

“Elias was not forgotten.”

“Were you the only one remembering him?”

Mara could not answer.

Elias had stopped visiting the village after their father died. There had been an argument at the funeral—something about the family cottage and old debts. Angry words. Months passed, then years. Mara had written letters, but fewer each winter. Elias had sent birthday cards until one year he did not.

She had meant to visit.

She had always meant to visit.

The forest opened onto a plain beneath a starless sky. Thousands of roads crossed it. Some were paved with gold bricks, others with shells, bones, broken clocks, or children’s wooden blocks. Staircases climbed into darkness. Bridges arched over dry land. Doorways stood without walls.

At every crossing, iron signposts pointed in impossible directions.

ROME, said one.

YESTERDAY, said another.

A third read HOME, though its arrow turned slowly in circles.

Mara unfolded her map. The road to the blue house was now a thread-thin line.

“Which way?” she asked.

Jonas pointed toward a path made of white tiles.

The moment Mara stepped onto it, she forgot why she had come.

She stood still, confused, lantern raised. Beside her waited a barefoot boy. In her hands lay a linen map.

“What is this place?” she asked.

Jonas seized her sleeve. “Say his name.”

“Whose name?”

“The person you’re looking for.”

Panic surged through her. There had been someone. A man laughing with a basket of apples.

“Elias,” she said.

The purpose of her journey returned in a rush.

They moved quickly. With each step, Mara repeated her brother’s name. The road tried to take other things instead.

She forgot the postman’s face.

She forgot the color of her kitchen walls.

She forgot the year her mother died.

Small memories lifted from her like sparks and drifted away. She saw them vanish into the darkness: her first day at school, the taste of snow, the tune Nessa had sung at her wedding.

“Elias,” Mara repeated. “Elias Vale.”

At the end of the white road stood a black gate.

Beyond it rose a mansion assembled from mismatched parts. A castle tower leaned against a farmhouse. Marble steps climbed to a ship’s door. Hundreds of chimneys pierced the roof, releasing streams of pale smoke filled with whispering voices.

“The House of Unremembering,” Jonas said.

The black gate opened.

“Are you coming?” Mara asked.

“No.”

“Why not?”

Jonas looked down at his bare feet.

“Because I belong to him.”

Before she could stop him, the boy ran into the dark. His red coat faded last.

Mara crossed the gate alone.

Inside the house, shelves stretched higher than lantern light. They held jars, boxes, books, bottles, and folded scraps of paper. Labels hung from each object.

THE LAST VERSE OF A SAILOR’S SONG.

THE LOCATION OF THREE BURIED BELLS.

THE REASON ANNA MARCH LEFT HOME.

THE TRUE NAME OF A STAR.

THE SMELL OF ELIAS VALE’S COAT AFTER RAIN.

Mara reached for the final jar.

“Please don’t touch the exhibits,” said a voice.

A tall man stood at the end of the aisle.

He wore a gray suit and white gloves. His hair was neither dark nor light, his face neither young nor old. Mara looked away for an instant and immediately forgot his features.

“You are the Collector,” she said.

“A crude title, but serviceable.”

“Where is my brother?”

“Which brother?”

“My only brother. Elias.”

The Collector smiled politely. “Names are unreliable. Come.”

He led her through the mansion.

They passed a room filled with portraits whose subjects had vanished from history. In another, glass birds sang extinct languages. A vast gallery contained doors from demolished houses. Behind each door, someone could be heard moving through rooms that no longer existed.

At last they entered a winter garden.

Snow fell beneath a painted ceiling. Bare trees grew from white ground. In the center stood the blue house.

Its paint was peeling. Warm light shone at the windows.

Mara ran to the front door and knocked.

A woman with red hair opened it.

For a moment Mara remembered Nessa singing at her wedding. Then the memory slipped away.

“Can I help you?” the woman asked.

“Nessa?”

The woman frowned. “My name is Ellen.”

A girl of perhaps fifteen appeared behind her. She had Elias’s dark eyes.

Mara felt tears rise.

“Lio,” she said.

The girl stepped back. “How do you know my name?”

“I’m your aunt.”

“I don’t have an aunt.”

Then Elias came down the stairs.

He was older, thinner, and bent in the shoulders. But he was Elias. Mara recognized the scar over his eyebrow, the way he held the banister, the irritated crease that appeared between his eyes when he was frightened.

“Elias,” she breathed.

He looked at her without recognition.

The Collector stood behind Mara.

“You see the difficulty,” he said.

“What did you do to them?”

“Very little. Forgetting is usually a communal effort.”

Elias gripped the doorframe. “Who is this?”

“Your sister,” said the Collector.

“I don’t have a sister.”

Mara stepped forward. “When you were nine, you climbed the mill roof because I said you were afraid. You fell through and broke your wrist. Father asked what happened, and I said the roof collapsed by itself.”

Elias stared at her.

“You carried apples backward along the ridge road,” she continued. “You gave me the cottage after Father died. I accused you of only doing it because you wanted to leave. We fought beside his grave.”

Something flickered in his expression.

“The cottage had a green door,” he whispered.

“Yes.”

“You hated green.”

“I still do.”

He touched the scar above his eyebrow.

“Mara?”

The winter garden trembled. Snow slid from the blue house roof. Somewhere in the mansion, glass shattered.

The Collector sighed.

“One memory is not enough,” he said. “He was forgotten by the village. Forgotten by former friends. Nearly forgotten by you. His wife had already misplaced her old name. His daughter’s childhood began dissolving. I rescued them before they disappeared entirely.”

“You imprisoned them.”

“I preserved them.”

“Why erase their memories?”

“To prevent longing. A preserved thing must remain still.”

Elias stepped from the house. “Can we leave?”

The Collector looked at Mara. “If she pays.”

“Pays what?”

“A road cannot lead away unless it leads from somewhere. To restore yours, another road must be surrendered.”

Mara clutched the linen map. “Take any road you like.”

“I do not choose payments. You do.”

The map unfolded by itself.

Its roads shone across the fabric: village lanes, mountain paths, coastal tracks. Mara saw every route she had ever drawn.

“What happens to the road I surrender?”

“It disappears. No one remembers what stood at its end.”

Mara thought of farmhouses, fishing huts, shrines, wells. Every road was tied to lives.

“I won’t erase someone else.”

“Then your brother stays.”

Nessa—Ellen—came to the doorway with Lio. Confusion clouded their faces. Elias looked at them, then at Mara.

“You should go,” he said quietly. “You came for me. That’s enough.”

“No.”

“Mara.”

“I spent twelve years planning to make things right. Planning is not the same as doing.”

The Collector watched with mild interest.

Mara studied the map.

In its lower corner, almost hidden beneath the stitched border, was a short road leading nowhere. She had drawn it as a child. It began at her father’s cottage, crossed an imaginary bridge, and ended at a castle in the sea. Her mother had helped color the towers red.

“That one,” Mara said.

The Collector leaned closer. “A childhood fancy?”

“Yes.”

“It is a road.”

“It leads nowhere real.”

“There is no such road.”

Mara hesitated. The imaginary castle had once been real to her. In winter, she had visited its hundred rooms. Her mother had been its queen, Elias its foolish knight, and Mara its mapmaker. On the castle’s highest tower, no one died, no one argued, and no one left.

“What will I forget?”

“Whatever waited at the end.”

Mara touched the tiny road.

She heard her mother laughing.

Not the weak laugh from the final winter, but the bright laugh from before illness. Her mother sat at the kitchen table, red pencil in hand, drawing flags on castle towers.

Every kingdom needs a way home, she had said.

Mara’s finger shook.

Then she looked at Elias. Already his recognition was fading. His face had begun to close.

“I choose this road,” she said.

The Collector placed one gloved hand over hers.

The imaginary road vanished.

For an instant Mara felt something tear open inside her. She saw red towers sinking beneath black water. She heard a woman call from a distant window, but she no longer knew who it was.

Then the vision was gone.

Mara looked at the blank corner of the map. She knew she had lost something precious, though she could not remember what.

The Collector bowed.

“Payment accepted.”

The blue house shuddered. Its walls folded inward like paper. Snow became rain. The garden trees burst into green leaves, and the black gate appeared at the end of a sunlit road.

Elias remembered her completely.

She saw it happen in his face: childhood, anger, absence, love.

He crossed the space between them and embraced her.

Behind him, Nessa gasped as her name returned. Lio began to cry, remembering birthdays, songs, and an aunt who had sent letters with maps drawn in the margins.

The Collector turned away.

“Wait,” Mara said. “The boy in the red coat. Jonas.”

He stopped.

“Who was he?”

“A forgotten child.”

“Why does he belong to you?”

“Because no one came looking.”

Mara thought of his bare feet beneath the hawthorn.

“I’m looking now.”

The Collector faced her. His features shifted like an image on disturbed water.

“You cannot claim what you do not remember.”

“I remember his name.”

“A name is not a life.”

“It’s a road.”

For the first time, the Collector looked angry.

Around them, the mansion groaned. Bottles rattled on distant shelves. The labels whispered.

Mara lifted the linen map. A new line had appeared, beginning at the House of Unremembering and ending somewhere in the dark.

“Jonas!” she shouted.

The name echoed through every room.

A red shape flashed between the winter trees.

“Jonas!” Elias called.

Nessa and Lio joined them.

Four voices became forty. The jars repeated the name. The extinct birds sang it. People behind vanished doors whispered it to one another.

Jonas.

The house shook.

The boy emerged from beneath a staircase, eyes wide. He ran through the snow and seized Mara’s hand.

The Collector reached for him, but the roads on the linen map blazed with golden light.

Every door in the mansion flew open.

Forgotten songs poured out first, flooding the halls with music. Lost faces stepped from portraits. Glass jars cracked, releasing scents, promises, birthdays, and names. A thousand roads unrolled through the walls, carrying exiles, ghosts, abandoned houses, and misplaced dreams toward places that had once loved them.

The Collector stood amid the storm, white gloves clenched.

“You will lose them again,” he shouted. “All of them! That is what people do!”

“Then we’ll remember them again,” Mara said.

She led her family through the gate.

They followed the white-tiled road across the plain, but now each step restored a memory instead of taking one. Mara remembered her kitchen walls, the postman’s face, her mother’s final winter. She remembered everything except what had stood at the end of the surrendered road.

At the black pines, dawn appeared between the branches.

Jonas stopped beneath the flowering hawthorn.

“Where will I go?” he asked.

“With us,” Mara said.

“For how long?”

“As long as the road allows.”

They crossed the north meadow at sunrise.

The road returned beneath their feet with a sound like rain. Hedges unfolded from the grass. Wheel ruts darkened the earth. The chapel bell rang once, though no one pulled its rope.

Villagers emerged from their houses.

The postman dropped his bag when he saw Elias. Mr. Bell shouted that he remembered delivering bread to the blue house. The schoolmistress began weeping because Lio had once sat in her classroom. Old Mrs. Lorne insisted she had never forgotten any of them, though everyone knew this was a lie.

By noon, the road was crowded with people traveling to welcome the lost family home.

Mara later redrew the village map. She made the ridge road darker than any other and labeled every bend. At Elias’s request, she added the blue house, though it now stood empty; he and his family chose to live near the village.

Jonas stayed with Mara.

No one discovered where he had come from. Some remembered a red-coated boy lost in a winter storm fifty years earlier. Others recalled a child who had wandered away from a traveling circus. Jonas himself offered a different story each time he was asked.

Mara did not mind. A mystery, she decided, was not the same as an absence.

Years passed.

New roads were built, old ones faded, and Mara mapped them all. In the attic, she opened the cedar boxes every winter and spoke the names written inside. Elias visited often. Nessa sang while Lio studied cartography. Jonas grew taller, though he never seemed to age as quickly as other children.

Sometimes Mara found herself staring at the blank corner of the linen map.

She knew a road had once been there. On quiet evenings, she almost remembered red towers, a bridge across the sea, and a woman’s hand guiding hers.

But the memory never fully returned.

So Mara drew a new road in its place.

It began at her cottage, passed the chapel, crossed the north meadow, and continued beyond the edge of the linen. She did not mark where it ended.

Underneath, she wrote:

**EVERY KINGDOM NEEDS A WAY HOME.**

She could not remember who had first said it.

Yet whenever she read the words, she felt the strange certainty that somewhere, beyond all mapped country, someone remembered her too.
